channel.title: OT/ICS Threat Intel - All Critical Infrastructure
channel.description: Curated OT/ICS advisories, incidents and threat intelligence. Editorial by Mike Holcomb in partnership with UtilSec.

item.title: [Critical] Washington puts federal cyber teams inside Texas water plants as July’s attacks are pinned at 30-plus Minnesota systems
item.description: The White House launched Project Watershed 250 on 31 August, a six-month pilot that places federal, state and vendor cyber teams inside Texas water utilities at no cost to the operator, with EPA and CISA as federal partners and Texas Cyber Command running red-team exercises against live utility networks. Officials say it is not a reaction to the July attacks, but the timing tells its own story: those intrusions reached more than 100 internet-exposed water systems, and Minnesota alone has now confirmed more than 30 affected community systems, with one city’s well and treatment plant shut down outright and two more forced to manual operation. For OT defenders the significance is not the funding. It is that the federal answer to internet-exposed PLCs is now an external red team, and the findings will set the template every other sector gets measured against. - Industrial Cyber reporting on the White House announcement, with Fox News Digital as the originating outlet and Tenable’s participation release — Minnesota impact detail from SecurityWeek, ABC News and Minnesota state officials - Programme announced 31 Aug 2026, reported 31 Aug–1 Sep 2026; underlying water intrusions 26–27 Jul 2026 with federal warnings late Jul 2026 — verified 2 Sep 2026, 6:21 PM ET

item.title: [Critical] The water campaign, quantified: 100+ exposed systems, and an attack surface no asset register had recorded
item.category: Campaign — Confirmed OT disruption, water sector
item.description: July’s wave against US water utilities is the best-documented OT campaign of the year, and CISA has now put a figure on it: malicious activity against more than 100 internet-exposed systems in the Water and Wastewater Systems sector, commonly programmable logic controllers wired straight into a cellular modem, with targeting reported across at least a dozen states including Minnesota, Michigan, South Dakota, Georgia, New Jersey and Alabama. The FBI records incidents at utilities in at least seven states since 27 July, some degrading operations — lost pressure, flooding, forced manual running — though supply was not widely interrupted. In some intrusions actors modified PLCs to disable shutdown processes and alarms, allowing unsafe conditions to develop unannounced. US officials assess Iranian actors as likely responsible and describe the activity as largely opportunistic. What makes this the board’s most useful item is the admission behind the number: the exposure that enabled it was in nobody’s asset register. - CISA exposure-reduction guidance and the FBI/EPA public service announcement — corroborated by SecurityWeek, TechCrunch and The Register - Scale confirmed and reported 26 Aug 2026; observed activity July 2026; FBI PSA issued late July 2026 — re-verified 2 Sep 2026, 6:21 PM ET

item.title: [High] A water-sector PLC maker was ransomed, and roughly 200 of its SCADA systems are reachable from the internet
item.category: Supply chain — Micro-Comm, water/wastewater PLC and SCADA supplier
item.description: Micro-Comm of Olathe, Kansas — which builds programmable logic controllers and the SCADAview CSX platform used by water and wastewater utilities — discovered a breach on 31 July and confirmed it publicly on 26 August, with the FBI investigating. The Barracuda ransomware group, a profit-motivated crew that says it is not state sponsored, published what it claims are nearly 850,000 stolen files totalling about 644 GB. Researchers reviewing the file listing report references to municipal customers, a US military facility, employee names and product documentation including system diagrams. The FBI has told the company it assesses the intrusion as opportunistic rather than targeted, and no manipulation of any customer’s control system has been reported. The number that should hold a water operator’s attention is a separate one: roughly 200 SCADAview CSX systems across US states are reachable from the public internet — the same exposure pattern that carried July’s campaign into more than 100 water systems. - Reuters exclusive of 26 Aug 2026 carrying company and FBI confirmation — corroborated by IBTimes and Newsmax; internet-exposure figure attributed to researchers cited in the reporting - Breach discovered 31 Jul 2026; disclosed 26 Aug 2026 — re-verified 2 Sep 2026, 6:21 PM ET

item.title: [High] The FBI seized the platform China used to hide inside other people’s routers — and the Department of Energy was on the target list
item.category: Nation-state — PRC obfuscation network built from compromised edge and IoT devices
item.description: The Justice Department and FBI announced court-authorised seizures of the domains behind QScan and QTRouter, two linked platforms run by a PRC state-sponsored group tracked as QTFY and operated out of Nanjing Xinjiuwei Network Technology Company. The mechanics matter more to OT than the indictment does. QScan sweeps the internet and automatically compromises thousands of IoT and embedded devices; QTRouter then chains those devices, commercial proxy services and leased servers into an obfuscation network that hides where an intrusion actually originates. Court documents describe QTFY selling that capability on to the Ministry of State Security and the People’s Liberation Army, across roughly eight years of activity. Named targets include the Department of Energy, NASA, the Federal Reserve, HHS, NIH and the US Senate. Black Lotus Labs calls the arrangement a quartermaster model — reconnaissance, proxy orchestration and routing sold as a service. - US Department of Justice Office of Public Affairs press release — corroborated by Cybersecurity Dive, Nextgov/FCW and Utility Dive, with technical detail from Lumen Black Lotus Labs - Seizure announced 26–27 Aug 2026; further reporting 1 Sep 2026 — verified 2 Sep 2026, 6:21 PM ET

item.title: [High] Congress’s own analysts say the water sector still has no enforceable cyber floor — five weeks after plants went manual
item.category: Congressional Research Service — Confirmed OT disruption, water sector
item.description: The Congressional Research Service has published an assessment of federal water-sector cyber protections in the wake of July’s attacks, and its finding is uncomfortable for anyone hoping the incident wave would be self-correcting: there is still no enforceable baseline cybersecurity requirement for community water systems, EPA’s 2023 attempt to fold cyber into sanitary surveys was withdrawn after litigation, and America’s Water Infrastructure Act risk assessments neither mandate controls nor are verified. The operational reality it is measuring against is now documented in detail: more than 30 Minnesota community systems hit on 26–27 July, Braham’s well and treatment plant temporarily shut down after computerised control was disabled, Plymouth and South St. Paul running manually, and Maple Plain declaring a local state of emergency. Roughly 150,000 US systems, most of them small, sit under that voluntary regime. - Congressional Research Service assessment as reported by Industrial Cyber, with the FBI/EPA public service announcement and Minnesota state and municipal confirmations — corroborated by SecurityWeek and ABC News - CRS analysis reported 31 Aug 2026; incidents 26–27 Jul 2026; FBI/EPA advisory 30 Jul 2026 — verified 2 Sep 2026, 6:21 PM ET

item.title: [High] Day nine at Boston Scientific: plants still disrupted by a breach that never reached a controller
item.category: Boston Scientific — Confirmed IT incident, production disrupted
item.description: Twelve days after detecting an intrusion on 25 August, Boston Scientific still has no full restoration date. Manufacturing, order processing and global shipping remain disrupted, with EDI and GHX orders queuing unfulfilled. The company’s 30 August update states that investigators have found no signs of malicious activity in its environment since detection, that the unauthorised access appears confined to certain on-premise systems rather than cloud, and that it hoped to resume shipping at least some products this week. CrowdStrike and other responders remain engaged. Implanted cardiac devices and established remote monitoring are unaffected. No entry route, vulnerability or ransomware involvement has been named, and no group has credibly claimed it. For OT defenders the lesson is unchanged and getting louder: an enterprise-side compromise that never touched a PLC has now disrupted production for the better part of a fortnight. - Boston Scientific incident page and SEC filing, plus SecurityWeek and Industrial Cyber recovery reporting — also covered by MedTech Dive, TechCrunch, Supply Chain Dive and CBS News - Detected 25 Aug 2026; disclosed 26 Aug 2026; manufacturing disruption confirmed 28 Aug 2026; company update 30 Aug 2026; still disrupted at 1 Sep 2026 per SecurityWeek recovery reporting — re-verified 2 Sep 2026, 6:21 PM ET

item.title: [Critical] NCSC: OT targeting is up across sectors globally, and it has already caused real-world disruption
item.category: Agency warning — Cross-sector OT targeting, real-world disruption
item.description: The UK’s National Cyber Security Centre published a statement on 27 August saying it is seeing increased targeting of operational technology across multiple sectors worldwide, including in the UK, carried out by a range of threat actors, and that this has already produced limited real-world disruption. The agency ties it to a broader pattern of disruptive activity against internet-exposed systems and edge devices — routers, gateways and firewalls that hand an attacker a foothold. Its asks are concrete: keep an accurate inventory of internet-facing systems, understand what each edge device does and where its data flows, patch promptly, retire end-of-life equipment, disable Telnet and SNMP v1/v2, and watch for unexpected configuration changes or outbound connections. Coming a day after CISA’s exposure guidance, this is two national agencies independently reaching the same conclusion in the same week. - UK NCSC news statement — corroborated by GovInfoSecurity and CircleID - Published 27 Aug 2026 — re-verified 2 Sep 2026, 6:21 PM ET

item.title: [Critical] A small UK generating station ran manually for four days after an Iran-linked cyberattack
item.category: Incident — Confirmed OT disruption, power generation (UK)
item.description: A small British power generating station was taken offline for four days by a cyberattack, with staff forced to restore operations manually. The Telegraph broke the story on 22 August; the UK government confirmed that a small-scale generator had been affected while stating there was at no point a risk to the national energy system, and the Department for Energy Security and Net Zero has since contacted power companies about the risk. UK assessments reported by the Telegraph point to hackers affiliated with the Iranian regime, likely the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps. The site’s size is the uncomfortable part rather than a reassurance: distributed generation, embedded generators and behind-the-meter assets sit below most reporting thresholds, are often remotely operated by a third party, and are numerous enough that an attack that works once is repeatable. - SecurityWeek and CNBC, both citing the originating Telegraph report and the UK government statement - Incident occurred July 2026; reported 22–23 Aug 2026; government response reported 24 Aug 2026 — re-verified 2 Sep 2026, 6:21 PM ET

item.title: [High] A frontier model ported a working PLC exploit to a second controller in eight hours — then bricked it
item.category: Forescout Vedere Labs — AI-assisted exploit development against PLCs
item.description: Forescout’s Vedere Labs published the result of a deliberately awkward experiment: point a frontier AI model at real industrial hardware and see how far it gets. Starting from the team’s own remote code execution exploit for a WAGO 750-852, built on CVE-2021-31886 — a pre-authentication overflow in the Nucleus FTP server — they asked Claude to port it to the related 750-831, giving the model a terminal, Ghidra and the physical device. It worked, but not cleanly. The first model tried failed to trace the vulnerable function; a stronger model eventually worked out why the injected shellcode was being wiped before it could run, and once past that it produced two working payloads in twelve minutes. Total cost of the final stage: over eight hours and more than $500 in API charges. A follow-up attempt at a command-and-control implant wrote to flash and permanently bricked the PLC. - Forescout Research – Vedere Labs report, via SecurityWeek — corroborated by Cybersecurity Dive with direct comment from Vedere Labs - Published 1 Sep 2026 — verified 2 Sep 2026, 6:21 PM ET

item.title: [High] Attacks meant to cause physical consequences rose last quarter — including a refrigerant release at a food plant
item.category: Kaspersky ICS CERT — Q2 2026 incident review, 163 publicly confirmed cases
item.description: Kaspersky ICS CERT’s quarterly review of industrial incidents, published 20 August, counts 163 cases publicly confirmed by the victims themselves in Q2 and flags a shift that matters more than the number: a marked rise in attacks intended to produce a physical consequence rather than data theft or extortion alone. The example it leads with is an Israeli food processing facility where an intrusion caused a refrigeration unit to fail and refrigerant to vent to atmosphere — an environmental and safety event, not an IT one. It sat inside a coordinated campaign, attributed by the researchers to an Iranian state-directed persona, that struck IT and OT together across defence, telecoms, fuel and transport logistics, and food production. Separate ransomware telemetry for the same quarter counts 1,140 incidents at industrial organisations, up 12% on Q1, with manufacturing absorbing 747 of them. For OT leaders the useful read is that the credible worst case has moved: increasingly a process consequence with a safety signature, not a fortnight of downtime. - Kaspersky ICS CERT quarterly incident overview — Q2 2026 ransomware volumes corroborated separately via Help Net Security - Report published 20 Aug 2026, covering Q2 2026 — verified 2 Sep 2026, 6:21 PM ET

item.title: [Medium] A battery-fleet attack would look exactly like a badly tuned controller — which is the whole problem
item.category: GRIDLOCK modelling — Cyber-physical exposure of grid-scale battery fleets
item.description: A risk assessment of grid-connected battery energy storage published on 2 September makes a detection argument before it makes a security one. Grid batteries earn money by reacting to system frequency — exporting when it sags, absorbing when it rises — so an attacker who nudges hundreds of them in the same direction generates a signal a control room reads as poor tuning or a settings error, right up to the moment the network starts shedding customers. The study is a Monte Carlo exercise, 10,000 simulations across three assumed industry security postures, and returns a 92% probability of a major attack on battery storage infrastructure by 2031 under industry-average practice, falling to 61.4% where operators certify against IEC 62443. It also prices the remedy, estimating roughly $0.8–2.8 billion to bring the ERCOT battery fleet to Security Level 2. Read the percentages as scenario output rather than forecast; the operational point survives either way, because the centralised optimiser and the manufacturer’s cloud control plane are single points of coordinated failure across an entire fleet. - Help Net Security analysis of the GRIDLOCK battery-storage risk assessment - Published 2 Sep 2026 — verified 2 Sep 2026, 6:21 PM ET

item.title: [Critical] SonicWall found attackers already inside its own remote-access gateway — a CVSS 10 pre-auth flaw chained to code execution
item.category: SonicWall SMA1000 — Two zero-days exploited, CVSS 10 chain
item.description: SonicWall disclosed on 1 September that two previously unknown vulnerabilities in its SMA1000 secure remote access gateway and SSL-VPN appliance have been exploited in the wild. CVE-2026-83548, carrying a CVSS score of 10, is a pre-authentication server-side request forgery in the Appliance Work Place interface that lets an unauthenticated attacker reach sensitive functionality; CVE-2026-83549, at 7.8, is an OS command injection flaw in the Appliance Management Console that an authenticated attacker can turn into remote code execution. SonicWall says it observed exploitation of both, which points to the pair being chained for unauthenticated code execution on the appliance. The vendor found the flaws and the attacks internally, and has published no indicators of compromise. Models 6210, 7210 and 8200v are affected. For OT operators this is the exact class of device that vendor engineers, integrators and on-call staff use to reach the plant from outside — a box that sits at the boundary, terminates trusted sessions and is rarely covered by an OT change window. - SonicWall PSIRT advisory SNWLID-2026-0016 — reported by SecurityWeek - Advisory published 1 Sep 2026, reported 2 Sep 2026 — verified 2 Sep 2026, 6:21 PM ET

item.title: [Critical] PaperCut attacks moved from scanning to human operators pivoting inside networks, and CISA set a 14 September deadline
item.category: PaperCut NG/MF — Exploited chain now in CISA KEV, hands-on-keyboard
item.description: The PaperCut NG/MF print-management flaws that the vendor first warned about on 27 August have escalated sharply. Exposure-management firm WatchTowr reports that activity has shifted from exploratory probing to real exploitation with hands-on-keyboard interaction, including tradecraft aimed specifically at pivoting from external to internal networks, and payloads keyed so only the original attacker can reuse the access — behaviour it associates with initial-access brokers. Two vulnerabilities, CVE-2026-82078 and CVE-2026-81578, are being chained by unauthenticated attackers to bypass authentication and execute code; PaperCut issued two emergency patches after the first was bypassed and is still working on a consolidated release. CISA added both to the Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalogue on 31 August with a federal remediation deadline of 14 September. ShadowServer counts more than 1,000 instances exposed to the internet. Print servers rarely appear on an OT risk register, yet they hold domain credentials and reach nearly every subnet in a plant. - CISA KEV catalogue addition of 31 August and the PaperCut security bulletin — escalation detail from WatchTowr via SecurityWeek, with Huntress and Rapid7 analyses - Vendor bulletin 27 Aug 2026; KEV addition 31 Aug 2026; escalation reported 1 Sep 2026 — verified 2 Sep 2026, 6:21 PM ET

item.title: [High] Five federal agencies say attackers are mapping Siemens S7 controllers with AI-written tools dressed as monitoring software
item.category: AA26-231A — Siemens S7 series PLCs, active reconnaissance
item.description: NSA, CISA, FBI, DOE and EPA issued a joint advisory on 19 August describing an active threat to Siemens S7 series programmable logic controllers in US critical infrastructure. The agencies say actors are using internet scanning services such as Censys and ZoomEye to locate exposed or poorly protected S7 devices, then running AI-generated exploitation scripts presented as legitimate OT monitoring tools. The scripts are built on the open-source snap7 and python-snap7 libraries, which speak S7comm natively — so the traffic looks like ordinary engineering activity. Coverage spans the full line from S7-200 through the S7-1500 F-series safety controllers, and the agencies name critical manufacturing, energy, water and wastewater, chemical, food and agriculture and commercial facilities as the most affected sectors. The assessed stage is reconnaissance and capability development, not confirmed manipulation. - CISA joint advisory AA26-231A, corroborated by BleepingComputer, The Hacker News, Industrial Cyber and Cybersecurity Dive - Advisory published 19 Aug 2026, still current — verified 2 Sep 2026, 6:21 PM ET

item.title: [High] CISA’s 1 September batch is five-sixths Rockwell — and it reaches the Logix controllers themselves
item.category: ICSA-26-244-01 to -05 — Five Rockwell advisories in one day, controllers included
item.description: CISA published eight ICS advisories on 1 September, and five of them are Rockwell Automation. The set covers RSLinx Classic (ICSA-26-244-01), the Redundancy Module Configuration Tool (-02), the Logix platform (-03), FactoryTalk Activation Manager (-04) and the ControlLogix, CompactLogix, CompactLogix 5480, GuardLogix and Compact GuardLogix controller families (-05). The RSLinx item is the one most sites will feel first: four flaws — CVE-2026-9621, CVE-2026-9622, CVE-2026-9624 and CVE-2026-9625 — let crafted Common Industrial Protocol traffic crash the communications service on version 4.50 and earlier, and it stays down until somebody restarts it by hand. RSLinx is the data path between controllers and the HMI, historian and engineering workstations, so a crash there is a visibility outage on a running process, not an IT inconvenience. The batch also carries an update to the Rockwell 1734 POINT I/O advisory (ICSA-26-202-09, Update A) and Update G to the long-running Mitsubishi Electric FA engineering software advisory (ICSA-24-135-04). - CISA ICS advisories ICSA-26-244-01 through -05 published 1 Sep 2026, plus ICSA-26-202-09 Update A and ICSA-24-135-04 Update G — corroborated against the Rockwell Automation security advisory index - Published 1 Sep 2026 — verified 2 Sep 2026, 6:21 PM ET

item.title: [Medium] The Coast Guard now has a single office that owns maritime cyber enforcement — expect the inspections to sharpen
item.category: US Coast Guard — Maritime Transportation System, enforcement
item.description: The US Coast Guard has stood up an Office of Maritime Cybersecurity Policy as the central authority for cyber policy across the Marine Transportation System, sitting under the Director of Inspections and Compliance. Its remit covers developing domestic policy for the cyber safety of ports, vessels and facilities, contributing to international standards, and — the line that matters operationally — directing a coordinated cybersecurity compliance and enforcement strategy. It also becomes the Coast Guard’s primary liaison to industry. For operators already working through the maritime cyber rule that entered force in 2025, this is the organisational signal that the discretionary phase is ending: a single office owning both policy and enforcement usually means more consistent inspection questions and less regional variation in how a deficiency gets written up. - US Coast Guard Maritime Commons announcement, reported by Industrial Cyber - Announced 31 Aug 2026; reported 1 Sep 2026 — verified 2 Sep 2026, 6:21 PM ET

item.title: [Medium] In nine days, anyone selling a connected product into the EU owes a 24-hour warning on exploited vulnerabilities
item.category: EU Cyber Resilience Act — Reporting obligations effective 11 Sep 2026
item.description: The EU Cyber Resilience Act enters its reporting phase on 11 September 2026. From that date, manufacturers of products with digital elements must report actively exploited vulnerabilities and severe security incidents affecting their products, with an early warning inside 24 hours and a fuller notification inside 72 hours. The scope reaches far past consumer IoT: PLCs, RTUs, drives, gateways, HMIs, protocol converters and the engineering software around them are products with digital elements, and the obligation follows the manufacturer regardless of where the affected device is installed. Legal analysts advise naming an owner now and building the assessment, escalation and customer-communication path in advance, coordinating it with existing NIS2 and GDPR duties rather than standing up a third parallel process. - Freshfields analysis via Lexology, surfaced in the Viakoo/Security Boulevard daily OT briefing - Analysis published 1 Sep 2026; obligations effective 11 Sep 2026 (forward-looking) — verified 2 Sep 2026, 6:21 PM ET

item.title: [High] A national emergency over foreign grid equipment — and it reaches the firmware, not just the transformer
item.category: Executive Order 14420 — Bulk-power system supply chain, US
item.description: On 26 August the President signed Executive Order 14420, declaring a national emergency under the International Emergency Economic Powers Act with respect to foreign-produced bulk-power system electric equipment. The order covers high-voltage infrastructure at or above 69 kV — transformers, inverters, generators and battery energy storage — and explicitly extends to associated software, firmware and remote-access capability. It prohibits transactions initiated after 26 August involving acquisition, importation, transfer or installation of covered equipment tied to designated foreign entities where the transaction poses a sabotage or disruption risk, and directs the Department of Energy to issue implementing rules within 120 days. Those rules may condition the continued operation of equipment already energised, and potentially require removal. For utilities this becomes a supply-chain compliance layer on top of NERC CIP-013, and it lands on a provenance record most operators do not have. - White House presidential action and fact sheet — legal analysis from Morgan Lewis and Troutman Pepper Locke; reporting from Utility Dive - Signed 26 Aug 2026; DOE implementing rules due within 120 days, by late Dec 2026 — re-verified 2 Sep 2026, 6:21 PM ET
